1

A Loudoun supervisor’s white paper estimated they received $895M in 2025 data center tax revenue, and Prince William County estimated $280 million.

2

Both the WHO (2021) and the American Heart Association treat the concentration-response relationship as monotonic down to the lowest measured exposures.

3

The IHME Global Burden of Disease 2023 estimates gives US PM2.5 at 69,774 and ozone at 12,843, so about 82,600 total. These overlap a bit, because PM2.5 and ozone affect some of the same diseases, so adding them up slightly double-counts. GBD’s combined “ambient air pollution” parent node corrects for that and lands in the same ballpark.

4

Fine particles stick around in the air for about 4–7 days before rain washes them out or they settle, which is plenty of time for wind to push them hundreds or thousands of miles. From this paper: “The all-models-average residence time is shortest for SS with about half a day, followed by SO4 and DU with four days, and POM and BC with six and seven days, respectively.”

5

GBD 2023 says about 13,000 US deaths a year are caused by ozone, with deaths almost entirely coming from COPD.

6

The American Lung Association says smoking causes “approximately 80 percent” of COPD deaths. The CDC gives the number as “as many as 8 out of 10.” For ozone, total US COPD deaths come to around 150,000, so 13,000 ozone deaths works out to about 10%.

7

EPA’s 2024 benefits document and BenMAP outputs usually put 85-95% of the dollar value from PM2.5/ozone cuts in avoided premature deaths. The rest is hospital visits, ER visits, asthma symptoms, and missed work or school.

8

One large cohort study followed 53 million US Medicare beneficiaries and found that a 10 ug/m3 increase in yearly average PM2.5 was associated with a 5% increase in all-cause mortality. Other major studies find it’s somewhere in the 5-8% range. This one finds 7.3%, this is 4-6%.

9

This is the largest multi-city short-term PM2.5 study and found about 0.68% additional all-cause mortality per 10 ug/m3 short-term PM2.5 increase. Per unit, these short-term effects are an order of magnitude smaller than the long-term coefficients described in footnote 7, partly because very quick spikes mostly bring forward deaths in already vulnerable people, whereas long-term exposure builds up new disease risk.

10

In the eastern U.S., every part-per-billion of NOx can produce about 1 to 7 parts-per-billion of ozone. The amount of PM2.5 nitrate creates is much smaller and depends a lot on ammonia availability. By mass, that implies much more ozone than nitrate PM2.5.

11

Daytime NOx lifetime is typically hours to about a day, mostly limited by OH oxidation of NO2 to HNO3 and other reservoir species, with longer effective lifetimes in winter and at higher latitudes. Wind at 5 to 15 mph carries it tens to a few hundred miles before it converts, which the EPA assumes happens in its interstate transport rules. The secondary PM2.5 it eventually forms with nitrate lingers in the air for longer as discussed in footnote 4, so PM2.5 impacts from NOx can show up much farther downwind than ozone impacts from the same source.

12

Coal is the only major US power source that contains significant sulfur. Natural gas has sulfur compounds removed before delivery, and oil is now a small part of US electricity. EPA Power Sector Data, EPA eGRID, and EIA electricity emissions data show coal causing the large majority of SO2 from the electricity sector recently.

13

US SO2 emissions are down about 95% from their peak in the late 70s and early 80s. The biggest wins in reducing SO2 were the Clean Air Act Acid Rain Program, the spread of air pollution control devices in coal plants (scrubbers), and coal-plant retirements. You can see the long run decline EPA’s Air Quality National Summary.

For how much the decline mattered for public health, see this study, which found that coal PM2.5 deaths among people receiving Medicare fell from around 43,000 a year between 1999 and 2007 to about 1,600 a year by 2020, roughly a 95% drop. The study attributes fewer deaths than some other models, here and here.

14

This study uses ambient NO₂ as a proxy for traffic pollution and finds that it caused about 134,000 new childhood asthma cases per year in the US, roughly 17.6% of all new childhood asthma. This study estimated that in the US, ozone is responsible for 8 to 21% of asthma ER visits and PM2.5 for 3 to 11%.

15

Each pathway has its own literature.

  • Heart attacks: this study found PM2.5 elevations within hours preceding MI onset in the Greater Boston area, large enough to detect in case-crossover designs.

  • Stroke: this study found a 34% increase in ischemic stroke odds within 24 hours of PM2.5 elevation, including at AQI levels EPA calls “moderate.”

  • Cognition: this study found faster long-term cognitive decline in older women with higher PM2.5 exposure; short-term studies find similar acute decrements in attention and working memory.

  • Daily mortality bumps: this study found about 0.68% additional daily all-cause mortality per 10 ug/m3 across 652 cities.

16

This meta-analysis of how pollutants drop off as you move away from roads found that NO₂ falls off within a few hundred meters, because the molecule either reacts with other things in the air (like ozone and OH) or just disperses.

17

US ambient NO₂ has dropped more than 50% at most monitoring sites since 2000. Both the annual mean limit (NAAQS: 53 ppb) and the standard for the 98th-percentile 1-hour daily maximum (100 ppb) are now well below the legal limits at almost all US sites. Getting this all from EPA Air Trends, Nitrogen Dioxide.

18

Standing right next to a wood fire can put you in a high-PM2.5 breathing zone. I use about 200 ug/m3 as a round, high-exposure value, which seems consistent with literature reviews on this. DC’s annual average PM2.5 is about 7.6 ug/m3 in AQLI and EPA AirData, so over a full year you breathe about 7.6 x 8,760 = 66,600 ug/m3-hours. One hour next to the fire adds about 200 - 7.6 = 192 extra ug/m3-hours, or 0.3% of the yearly total.

19

This study estimated total US PM2.5 exposure from human sources to be about 6.5 µg/m³ in 2014, and the national average to be 8 µg/m³, so natural sources made up about 15 to 20%. This study found that since 2016, wildfire smoke has wiped out about 25% of the multi-decade progress in cutting PM2.5, and more than 50% in many western states. So the natural share is rising.

20

In EPA’s 2020 National Emissions Inventory, wildland fires (both wildfires and prescribed burns) have overtaken every other category as the biggest source of primary PM2.5 emissions in the US, ahead of residential wood burning, road dust, and industrial sources. Three other studies back this up, here here and here.

21

US “background” ozone, meaning ozone not from domestic human NOx/VOC emissions, is roughly 25-50 ppb, versus typical summer surface ozone of 50-70 ppb. That puts background around 40-70% in many regions, especially the West and higher elevations. Purely natural ozone is lower, more like 30-50%, because it excludes global human emissions and uses preindustrial methane. Discussed here and here.

22

GBD 2023 estimates have ambient PM2.5 at about 7-8% of global deaths and 5% of DALYs. In the US, it is about 1.7-2% of deaths and 1.5-2% of DALYs.

23

This is why I use 3-4 years for PM2.5. In their Medicare analysis, the average elderly person whose death is attributed to PM2.5 had about 3.6 years of remaining life expectancy. GBD methods give more like 10-14 years, but they do not adjust for the fact that pollution deaths often exacerbate previous medical conditions in people who were more close to dying, so I use 3-4 years to adjust.

24

Using AQLI, DC’s PM2.5 is about 7.6 ug/m3 and the rural US average is about 6.7, a gap of 0.9. AQLI’s 0.098 years lost per ug/m^3 gives 0.09 years, or 33 days, so “about a month.” That coefficient comes out of cohort work like Pope et al. 2002, Di et al. 2017, and Wang et al. 2020. Using the method here gives more like 6 days.

25

1970 pickup trucks were certified at about 3.4 grams per mile of non-methane hydrocarbons under the federal standards at the time, when there were no catalytic converters and engines were carbureted. Modern Tier 3 Bin 50 light trucks have to keep NOx and NMOG combined under 0.05 g/mi, with a target of 0.030 g/mi NMOG+NOx by 2025. That’s about a 98-99% reduction in tailpipe non-CO2 pollution. Sources: EPA Tier 3 standards, EPA Green Vehicle Guide, and EPA’s history of transportation emissions reductions.

26

Leaf-blower PM depends on whether you count only exhaust or also dust. For the truck, EPA MOVES and CARB put 300 miles from a modern light truck at only a few grams of PM2.5. For the blower, CARB and this study support a high combined exhaust-plus-dust value around 15 g/hour. Compared with about 4 g from the truck, that is about 4x. This article is useful color, but not the PM2.5 source.

27

10,000 cars x 5,000 miles x about 0.010 g/mi total PM2.5 is about 500 kg. The car PM number comes from EPA MOVES plus this study for non-exhaust PM. Roughly, that equals about one hour of NYC commercial cooking, 2-3 days from a mid-sized cement plant, one day from a cruise ship at berth, or 10 wood-heated homes for a winter. Those comparisons use linked NYC, EPA, ICCT/EPA, and wood-smoke sources.

28

The 2024 Corolla LE gets 38 mpg combined. Using EPA’s 8,887 g CO2 per gallon of gasoline, that’s 234 g CO2/mile, or 2.8 tons/year at average US mileage. It is Tier 3 Bin 50 certified, so NOx and NMOG is around 0.05 g/mi. For PM2.5, a lot’s created by brake and tire wear, which OECD puts at 30-60 mg/mile. EASIUR puts the local US health damage at maybe $10-$25/year. The CO2 side is about $42/year from this study’s estimate that every ton of CO2 mitigated gets $15.1 in wildfire health savings, or $60-$85 if you include ozone, dust, and stagnation. So CO2 does about 2-8x more US air damage than the car’s direct emissions, and >10x globally.

29

A modern gas plant emits about 360 kg CO2/MWh. Pollution is roughly 36 g NOx and 12 g PM2.5 per MWh (with good NOx controls and EPA’s PM2.5 factor). This model estimates local health damage around $1-$2/MWh. This study finds the US-only wildfire health cost of the CO2 from gas at about $5.40/MWh, or more with other climate-air effects and global impacts. So CO2 does about 3-10x more US air damage than stack pollution.

30

This study says CO2-driven wildfire smoke damages are much bigger globally than in the US, they’re about $15/ton here versus around $100/ton globally. Obviously this makes sense, the world’s big!

31

US coal power fell from about 966 TWh in 2019 to about 635-653 TWh in 2024, a 32-33% drop. The numbers come from this EIA table and this EIA table.

32

EPA’s central value of a life is $7.4 million in 2006 dollars. About $12 million in 2026 dollars.

33

EPA’s 2024 benefits document and BenMAP outputs usually put 85-95% of the dollar value from PM2.5/ozone cuts in avoided premature deaths. The rest is hospital visits, ER visits, asthma symptoms, and missed work or school.

34

In 2003, EPA tried a lower VSL for people over 70 in its Clear Skies analysis. Critics called it the “senior death discount,” and EPA dropped it. This article covers this.

35

Open fireplaces emit roughly 10-17 g of primary PM per kg of wood, mostly PM2.5, using EPA AP-42 Chapter 1.9 and its fireplace emission-factor background. Note that this is measuring outdoor air pollution, not what people in the homes breathe. A 5 kg evening is about 50-85 g; Shlipak et al. 2026 in Science Advances gets about $99B in damages over 485,000 tons of residential-wood PM2.5, or roughly $200K/ton, so that evening is about $10-$17. Almost all of that is health damage, not climate damage, because biogenic CO2 is roughly carbon-neutral over regrowth time. NOAA repository copy.

36

This HHS document puts VSLY at $604K with a 3% discount rate and $1.006M with 7%, in 2024 dollars for 2025 impacts. The method comes from HHS guidance. I use $550K as a conservative round number: below the 3% figure and about 10% lower than the downstream estimates would otherwise be.

37

4,000-9,000 annual US deaths from fossil power-plant PM2.5 comes from this modeling and this study, most of it is coming from coal. Using IHME GBD 2023’s 21.2 DALYs per air-pollution death, that is about 85,000-190,000 DALYs, or $47B-$105B/year at the $550K/DALY from FN35. Deryugina et al. 2019 would instead give about 14,000-32,000 life-years and $8B-$18B/year, but I use GBD here so the dollar comparisons stay apples-to-apples with COBRA.

38

About 1.2 million New England homes burn wood at all, from EIA’s RECS tables and this EIA summary. Scaling EPA NEI emissions and this study gives about 270-360 deaths/year, or $3B-$4B, if you count all wood-burning homes. Counting only primary wood-heating homes gives about 130 deaths and $1.5B. Big uncertainty: supplemental burning, local dose-response, and cross-state smoke. The adjustment mentioned in FN36 would shrink it about 5-6x.

39

In Ohio v. EPA, the Supreme Court put the 2023 Good Neighbor Plan on hold on June 27, 2024 while litigation continued. EPA later moved into reconsideration and announced a proposed action on January 28, 2026. EPA’s live Good Neighbor and interstate-transport pages are the current status. As of May 2026, the plan is not being enforced in its original strong form.

40

This study tracked Medicare data and found a 7.3% higher all-cause mortality risk per 10 ug/m3 more long-term PM2.5, or about 0.73% per 1 ug/m3. This study and this study find Black-white PM2.5 exposure gaps around 1.4-2.0 ug/m3, which works out to about 1-1.5% extra all-cause mortality risk from PM2.5 alone.

This study found PM2.5 exposure lowered overall from 2010 to 2019, but relative racial gaps widened. In 2019, the least-white census tracts had 16% higher PM2.5 than the most-white tracts, and ethnic relative disparities in PM2.5-attributable mortality grew by 40%. This copy has the repository version.

42

This study estimates about 17,900 US deaths/year from agriculture-related PM2.5, including about 15,900 from food production. Animal-based foods cause about 80% of the food-production damage, or about 12,700 deaths. The study says on-farm fixes could cut food-production mortality by about half, so rounding that to 6,000.

43

The range comes from two estimates, this that gets around 900, and this that’s closer to 2000.

44

Residential wood burning is about 10-17% of US anthropogenic PM2.5 mortality across this, this, and this study. The spread is mostly caused by differences in thinking on secondary PM2.5, indoor vs outdoor exposure, and wildfire vs anthropogenic wood. This residential wood-heating overview says wood provides 2.2% of residential energy but 98% of residential-combustion PM2.5, implying roughly 1,000x more PM2.5 per unit of residential energy.

Fertilizer-fed soil microbes turn ammonium and nitrate into NO and N2O. The NO escapes and becomes NO₂, as EPA’s CMAQ docs on soil microbial NOx emissions explain. This study estimated soil microbes were 20-32% of Central Valley NOx during the growing season. For ways of controlling these better see this agricultural nitrogen management options review plus this article.
